title: I only show the way
hookLine: the gradual training, like an accountant's method; some arrive, some don't; I only show the way

lines: ONE, TWO, THREE, UP TO A HUNDRED.
cards: Moggallāna the accountant, a brahmin, not the well-known monk of the same name, is visiting the Buddha at a palace-monastery in Sāvatthī. He notices the staircase.
In this building, he says, you can see a gradual progress, step by step, all the way to the top stair. Our brahmin studies are like that. So is archery.
And in my trade, accounting, we teach a student to count step by step: one, two, three, on up to a hundred. Is there anything like that in your teaching?

teach.b: There is, says the Buddha. Like a skilled horse trainer with a fine colt, I start a person with the first step: live by the precepts, see the danger in small faults.

Then guard the senses: when you see a shape, don't grab at it. Eat in moderation, not for fun or show, just enough to keep the body going. Be wakeful, walking and sitting by day and in the early night.
Be mindful in everything, going out and coming back, eating, dressing, speaking, keeping silent.
Then a quiet place, a forest or the foot of a tree, the body upright, the hindrances let go, and deep stillness, one stage after another. Then Moggallāna asks the harder question.
Does everyone you teach reach the goal? No, the Buddha says. Some do, some don't.
Why not, if the path is there and you're there to guide it?

Suppose someone asks you the way to Rājagaha. You tell them clearly: go this way, you'll see a village, then a town, then Rājagaha itself, with its parks and ponds. One person follows the directions and arrives.
Another takes the wrong road. Whose fault is that? The city is there.
The road is there. You were there to point.
And the Buddha says: the Tathāgata only shows the way. The Dhammapada says it in Max Müller's words: "You yourself must make an effort. The Tathâgatas (Buddhas) are only preachers."

how: Buddhist teachers commonly describe themselves as guides rather than saviors, and students are taught the path in stages, from keeping precepts to guarding the senses, mindfulness and meditation.

o: the Buddha's word for himself as a guide
a king who rules the world by the teaching
a god who carries people to the far shore

games.q: the accountant's question: tap the pairs.
p: just enough to keep the body going
some arrive, some take a wrong turn

s: the accountant in this sutta is the well-known monk Moggallāna
he's a brahmin accountant with the same name.
the Buddha says everyone he teaches reaches the goal
some do and some don't: he only shows the way.
the Dhammapada says 'you yourself must make an effort'
in Müller's words: 'the Tathâgatas (Buddhas) are only preachers.'

games.q: you give someone clear directions to Rājagaha. they take the wrong road. whose fault does the Buddha say that is?
o: yours, for not walking them there
not the road's, and not the guide's: the walking is theirs
the city's, for being hard to find
games.why: the city is there, the road is there, and the guide pointed. the Tathāgata, he says, only shows the way.

practice: Picture whatever path you're on as a road with landmarks, and see where you are now: by the village, or the town.
Don't measure how far it is to the city; just see the next small step, a precept kept more carefully, a meal eaten mindfully, a little longer sitting, and breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: Tathagata, the Buddha's word for himself as one who only shows the way. The gradual training is there, step by step like counting, but the walking is up to each person.

orig.note: Pali maggakkhāyī: one who points out the path, the Buddha's word for himself here.

carryVoice: Your line: the walking is yours. The teacher points, and the road stays open. That's day four eighty-one.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
sources.q: You yourself must make an effort. The Tathâgatas (Buddhas) are only preachers.
